Text 1 — Novel Extract: Adapted from Chapter 1 of The House
of the Spirits by Isabel Allende
Barrabés came to us by sea, the child Clara wrote in her delicate calligraphy. She was already
in the habit of writing down important matters, and afterward, when she was mute, she also
recorded trivialities, never suspecting that fifty years later I would use her notebooks to
reclaim the past and overcome terrors of my own. Barrabas arrived on a Holy Thursday. It
was a bland, autumnal day that gave no hint of the events that the child would record, which
took place during the noon mass in the parish of San Sebastian. As a sign of mourning, the
statues of the saints were shrouded in purple robes. Beneath these funereal sheets the celestial
retinue! resembled nothing so much as a roomful of furniture awaiting movers, an impression
that the candles, the incense, and the soft moans of the organ were powerless to counteract.
The only one whose appearance was enhanced by mourning was the church’s patron saint,
Sebastian, for during Holy Week the faithful were spared the sight of that body twisted in the
most indecent posture, pierced by arrows, and dripping with blood and tears like a suffering
homosexual, whose wounds, kept miraculously fresh by Father Restrepo’s brush, made Clara
tremble with disg
Severo del Valle was an atheist and a Mason, but he had political ambitions and could not
allow himself the luxury of missing mass on feast days, when everyone would have a chance
to see him. His wife, Nivea, preferred to deal with God without benefit of intermediaries. She
had a deep distrust of cassocks? and was bored by descriptions of heaven, purgatory and hell,
but she shared her husband’s parliamentary ambitions, hoping that if he won a seat in
Congress she would finally secure the vote for women. Clara, the youngest of her children,
was seated beside her mother, who squeezed her hand impatiently whenever the priest
lingered too long on the sins of the flesh, for she knew that this would only lead the child to
visualise with even greater accuracy aberrations’ that transcended reality.
Just at that moment, as Nivea would recall years later, in the midst of all that anxiety and
silence, the voice of little Clara was heard in all its purity.
“Psst! Father Restrepo! If that story about hell is a lie, we’re all fucked, aren’t we...?”
The Jesuit’s index finger, which was already raised to illustrate additional tortures, remained
suspended like a lightning rod above his head. People stopped breathing. Sefior and Sefiora
del Valle reacted first. Severo grabbed his wife by the arm and Clara by the neck and walked
out, followed by the rest of the children, who stampeded toward the door.
By Isabel Allende
Retinue: a group of people who accompany and support an important person, often in a formal or ceremonial
context. This group may include assistants, advisers, attendants, or followers.
2 Cassocks: a long, close-fitting, ankle-length robe worn by members of the clergy or other church officials,
often as part of their official or ceremonial dress.
5 Aberrations: something that deviates from what is normal, expected, or accepted — often in a way that is
unusual, strange, or unsettling,
Text 2 - Critical Extract: ‘At the Threshold of Memory: Isabel Allende’s
World-Building in The House of the Spirits’
From the opening line — “Barrabas came to us by sea” — Isabel Allende begins not just a
narrative, but the shaping of a literary world steeped in memory, ritual, and quiet subversion.
In the first scene of Chapter 1, this world is rendered with precision and resonance, drawing
the reader into a space where the familiar is made strange, and the personal is inseparable
from symbolic structures of power.
Set during a Holy Thursday mass,
the church is evoked through layered s
nsory detail —
incense, candlelight, silence, and purple-shrouded sain
s. The space appears
sacred, yet
Allende quietly undermines its authority. Saint Sebastian is rendered grotesque, and the
statues appear lifeless, “like furniture awaiting movers.” This technique recalls Mikhail
Bakhtin’s concept of the carnivalesque, where dominant structures of meaning — religious,
moral, political — are momentarily suspended or inverted, revealing their instability
(Rabelais and His World, 1965). Allende’s world is thus not stable or reverent, but one in
tension — a site of theatrical control and latent resistance.
Characterisation deepens this world’s complexity. Severo, a political aspirant, performs
piety without belief. Nivea endures the constraints of gendered expectation, her internal
monologue filled with scepticism. These figures position the reader within a social order
defined by performance and contradiction. In this way, Allende enacts what Linda Hutcheon
describes as the function of historiographic metafiction: the destabilisation of historical
"truth" through a blending of narrative voice, irony, and personal perception (4 Poetics of
Postmodernism, 1988).
Clara, the youngest daughter, quietly occupies the centre of this world. We learn she is,
already recording “important matters” — an act that will later shape the novel’s structure.
Clara’s narrative presence links the present scene to an act of remembering, positioning the
entire fictional world as
something constructed through retrospection. As Elizabeth Waites
notes, Clara “mediates the novel’s sense of time, making the personal past continuous and
accessible” (Latin American Women Writers, 1996). The act of remembering becomes a
mode of world-building — a way of recovering and reshaping experience through written
reflection.
At the chapter’s climax, Clara’s question — “If that story about hell is a lie, we're all
fucked, aren’t we...?” — ruptures the world’s ceremonial order. Her child’s voice deflates
ecclesiastical authority, disarming not only Father Restrepo, but the entire congregation.
This moment aligns with Wolfgang Iser’s theory of “blanks” in the text: moments where
narrative structure opens itself to reader interpretation, disrupting expectation and provoking
reflection (The Act of Reading, 1978). Through Clara, the text inserts an interpretive void —
a moment of irreverence that reconfigures the reader’s understanding of the moral and
ideological framework previously established.
Tzvetan Todorov has argued that the fantastic emerges in literature where uncertainty
between the real and the unreal is sustained (The Fantastic, 1973). Allende’s world hovers
in this ambiguity — grounded in sensory realism but edged with the spectral, shaped as
much by perception and memory as by action.
In just one scene, Allende constructs a world where ritual is strained, language resists
closure, and voice becomes a mode of rebellion. This is a world born from memory, but one
ind by the act of
in which meaning is continually negotiated — by characters, by reader
storytelling itself.
By A. S. Calderén
